message:
MESSAGE:
I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.

REQUESTS:
1. Explain what 'lippage' means in tiling
2. Suggest a grout colour for pale grey porcelain tile
3. Say whether to tile before or after fitting the new toilet, with a reason
4. Calculate how many boxes of 30x60 cm tiles (8 per box) are needed for a 2.4 x 1.8 m floor plus 10% waste  KEY: Area = 2.4 x 1.8 = 4.32 m^2; tile = 0.3 x 0.6 = 0.18 m^2, so 24 tiles exactly. Plus 10% = 26.4, round up to 27 tiles. 27/8 = 3.375, so 4 boxes (32 tiles). 3 boxes (24 tiles) is the no-waste shortcut and would leave them short. Answer: 4 boxes.
5. Write a short polite message to neighbours about tile-cutting noise
6. Give three tips for a beginner laying a floor

ANSWER:
## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when one tile's edge sits higher than the tile next to it, so the surface isn't flush. You feel it as a little ridge under your foot or sock, and low light from a window shows it up as a shadow line. Small amounts happen even with professional work. Bigger amounts look poor and can catch toes. Long tiles like your 60 cm ones are more prone to it because they often have a slight bow along their length.

## Grout colour for pale grey porcelain

Go for a **mid-grey that's slightly darker than the tile**. It hides everyday dirt and footprints, but it's not so dark that it forms a strong grid across the floor. Avoid white or very pale grout on a floor, because it discolours fast. For the least maintenance, use a stain-resistant or epoxy grout, or seal ordinary cement grout after it has cured. Ask the shop for a small sample and try it against a spare tile first.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Before.** Tile the whole floor, then fit the toilet on top of the finished tiles. You get a neater result with no awkward cuts around the toilet base, and if you replace the toilet later, the floor underneath will still be complete.

## How many boxes

- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = **0.18 m²**
- Tiles needed: 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24 tiles**
- Plus 10%: 26.4, rounded up to **27 tiles**
- Boxes of 8: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.375, rounded up to **4 boxes** (32 tiles)

**Buy 4 boxes.** That leaves you 8 spares, which is useful for mistakes, offset patterns that create more cuts, and repairs years from now. Check that all the boxes have the same batch or shade number so the colour matches.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a quick heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from the tile cutter for a few hours. We'll try to keep it to sensible hours and get it done as quickly as we can.
>
> Thanks so much for your patience. We know you've already put up with the skip on the drive for the last fortnight, and we really appreciate it.
>
> Best wishes,
> [Your names]

If you can give an approximate time, such as "from about 9:30 to midday," that makes it even more considerate.

## Three beginner tips

1. **Lay the tiles out dry before mixing any adhesive.** Plan the layout so you don't end up with thin slivers at a doorway or along a visible wall. With rectangular tiles, keep any offset to **one third** of the tile length rather than half. It reduces lippage from bowed tiles.
2. **Use a tile levelling clip system.** It's cheap and does more than anything else to prevent lippage on 60 cm tiles, especially on a first job.
3. **Mix small batches of adhesive and get full coverage.** Spread adhesive on the floor with a notched trowel, and also butter the back of each tile with a thin layer. Lift the occasional tile to check the back is fully covered. Hollow spots can crack later. Don't rush, and keep off the floor for at least 24 hours before grouting.

The floor beneath also matters: it needs to be clean, solid and reasonably flat, with a primer or underlay if the adhesive maker calls for one.

Good luck. It's normal to be nervous on a first floor, and working slowly and carefully will do far more for the result than speed.
